verses.text: Now Yahweh said to Abram, “Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father’s house, and go to the land that I will show you.
I will make of you a great nation. I will bless you and make your name great. You will be a blessing.
I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who curses you. All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.”
So Abram went, as Yahweh had told him. Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran.

Abram took Sarai his wife, Lot his brother’s son, all their possessions that they had gathered, and the people whom they had acquired in Haran, and they went to go into the land of Canaan. They entered into the land of Canaan.
Abram passed through the land to the place of Shechem, to the oak of Moreh. The Canaanites were in the land, then.
Yahweh appeared to Abram and said, “I will give this land to your offspring.”  He built an altar there to Yahweh, who had appeared to him.
He left from there to go to the mountain on the east of Bethel and pitched his tent, having Bethel on the west, and Ai on the east. There he built an altar to Yahweh and called on Yahweh’s name.
Abram traveled, still going on toward the South.
There was a famine in the land. Abram went down into Egypt to live as a foreigner there, for the famine was severe in the land.
When he had come near to enter Egypt, he said to Sarai his wife, “See now, I know that you are a beautiful woman to look at.
It will happen, when the Egyptians see you, that they will say, ‘This is his wife.’ They will kill me, but they will save you alive.
Please say that you are my sister, that it may be well with me for your sake, and that my soul may live because of you.”
When Abram had come into Egypt, Egyptians saw that the woman was very beautiful.
The princes of Pharaoh saw her, and praised her to Pharaoh; and the woman was taken into Pharaoh’s house.
He dealt well with Abram for her sake. He had sheep, cattle, male donkeys, male servants, female servants, female donkeys, and camels.
Yahweh afflicted Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai, Abram’s wife.
Pharaoh called Abram and said, “What is this that you have done to me? Why didn’t you tell me that she was your wife?
Why did you say, ‘She is my sister,’ so that I took her to be my wife? Now therefore, see your wife, take her, and go your way.”
Pharaoh commanded men concerning him, and they escorted him away with his wife and all that he had.

footnotes.content: I still marvel that the Lord first calls Abram away before He tells him all the details. He asks for his country, relatives, and father's house — the very things a man would lean on for security. Yet the God who calls him is also the God who says, 'I will show you,' so the leaving is done by faith in the One who leads.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: How kind of Yahweh to promise to make Abram great, bless him, and make his name great — not for Abram's glory alone, but so that he would be a blessing. I learn here that God's blessings are meant to flow through us to others, not stop with us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord binds Himself to Abram in a way that touches every family on earth. I see here the first glimmer of a blessing that would one day come through Abram's offspring for all nations. My old heart takes comfort that God's promise of blessing reaches far beyond one man.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seventy-five years old, and Abram goes as Yahweh told him. Lot goes with him, but the obedience starts with Abram. I take courage that it is never too late for a man to walk in simple faith when the Lord says 'go'.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abram takes his whole household — Sarai, Lot, their possessions, and the people they had acquired in Haran — and sets out for Canaan. It is a costly move: leaving what was gained to go to what was promised. Faith often packs up everything it has to follow the God who provides.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abram passes through to Shechem, to the oak of Moreh, and the Canaanites are still in the land. The promise says 'I will give this land,' yet at that moment it belongs to another. I learn to trust God's word even when the land of promise is occupied by those who do not know Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh appears to Abram and gives the promise directly: 'I will give this land to your offspring.' Abram's response is worship — he builds an altar to the God who appeared to him. When God speaks a promise to a fearful heart, the natural thing for faith is to build an altar and give Him praise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abram moves to the mountain between Bethel and Ai, pitches his tent, and builds another altar to Yahweh, calling on His name. He is a pilgrim with no land of his own yet, but he knows exactly where to turn. A man with no inheritance still has the God who is his portion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abram continues toward the South, still journeying. The promise is sure, but he has not arrived. I am reminded that God's people often live between the promise given and the promise fulfilled, walking by faith one step at a time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A famine comes to the land God just promised to give him. Abram goes down to Egypt to live as a foreigner. Even the man of faith finds that following the Lord does not spare him from hard providences. Yet the God who promised the land is still faithful in the famine.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As Abram nears Egypt, he sees Sarai's beauty with fear for his own life. How quickly a man who just built altars to Yahweh can begin to lean on his own cleverness for protection. I see my own weakness here, and I need the God who is better able to protect His servant than the servant is to protect himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abram's fear is real: in a foreign land, a beautiful woman could cost him his life. But fear is leading him to trust Pharaoh more than the God who called him and promised to bless him. The God who said 'I will bless you' is the same God Abram is forgetting to trust in this moment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abram asks Sarai to say she is his sister so that it may be well with him. In doing so, he seeks to protect himself at the cost of exposing Sarai to great danger. It grieves me to see faith falter, but it also makes me thankful for a greater Abram — Jesus — who would never save Himself by endangering others, but would save others by giving Himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As Abram feared, the Egyptians see Sarai and see she is very beautiful. The plan born of fear is now beginning to bear the very fruit he hoped to avoid. How often we make a mess trying to protect what God has already promised to guard.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh's princes praise Sarai to Pharaoh, and she is taken into his house. Abram's scheme puts Sarai in the power of a pagan king. I am thankful that the God who made the promise is not bound by Abram's failure, and that He will act to preserve both Sarai and the seed of promise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh deals well with Abram for Sarai's sake, giving him sheep, cattle, donkeys, servants, and camels. Ironically, Abram gains wealth by the very lie that endangered his wife. The blessings of God were promised freely, but here they come tangled in the consequences of unbelief.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh himself intervenes, afflicting Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai, Abram's wife. The Lord is jealous to protect the woman through whom the promised Seed would come. I take comfort that when His people are in danger through their own folly, He still defends the promise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh confronts Abram with a stinging question: 'What is this that you have done to me?' The man of God is rebuked by a pagan king for his lack of truthfulness. May the Lord give us grace to trust Him so fully that we have no need to deceive to be safe.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh asks why Abram said Sarai was his sister, making him take her as his wife. With gentle authority he tells Abram to take his wife and go. I see God's mercy: even after Abram's failure, He brings him out of Egypt with Sarai restored and the promise still intact.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh commands his men to escort Abram, Sarai, and all he has out of Egypt. The Lord uses even an unbelieving king to deliver His servant and preserve His promise. After a shameful chapter of fear and failure, the faithful God brings Abram back toward the land He promised to give him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
